units: a wall painting decays because its support soaks up water
the colored layer flakes away from the wall
the damage comes from the support and not from the paint
the first step is to draw the moisture out of the wall
compresses pull the salts out of the wall
the loose fragments are set back down with a liquid adhesive
the losses are filled with fine hatching that can be spotted up close
the missing decoration is not painted back in
text: Picture a painted wall shedding itself while you watch. The plaster drinks in the damp, the color lifts, and the wall painting some long-gone workshop laid down there crumbles into dust. Blame almost never falls on the paint. The trouble sits behind it, in a support that swells and shifts. So the conservators dry the wall out first, slowly, laying on compresses that pull the salts up out of the masonry. Then they go after the flakes, one at a time, slipping a thin liquid adhesive under every lifted chip until it settles back down. Brushes come last, and barely. They fill the losses with fine hatching, close-set strokes that anyone leaning in can spot for what they are. No serious workshop paints the lost decoration back in. You stabilize, you fill, you leave the wound legible, and the work stands there owning up to what happened to it.

units: an exhibition separates the finished work and its preparatory drawings into two rooms
the finished painting is shown alone on a dark wall
visitors speak quietly in front of the finished painting
the preparatory drawings are hung close together and show second thoughts
the public stops longer in front of the preparatory drawings
the preparatory drawings start conversations between visitors
a teacher believes her students finally grasp that creation happens step by step
the organizer of the exhibition hesitated to show the working documents
text: The split hits you at the door. One room holds the finished painting and nothing else, hung alone on a dark wall, lit hard from above, and people drop their voices as they walk in. The next room does the opposite. The preparatory drawings crowd the wall, pinned edge to edge, full of second thoughts, lines abandoned halfway, thumb smudges along the margins. The guards will tell you where the crowd actually stops. The finished canvas gets silence. The sketches get talk, strangers pointing things out to one another. A teacher who came with her class put it plainly. Her students had finally understood that a picture is not handed over whole, that it gropes and fails and starts again. The man who built the show admits he nearly kept that second room shut, afraid of stripping the wonder off the thing he was showing.

units: the modeling material must first be softened under the hands
the air bubbles are driven out by slamming the mass on a hard surface
a dull sound shows that the air has been forced out
the thumbs hollow the piece out from the center
the fingers draw the wall upward
the drying happens in the shade under a damp cloth
drafts must be avoided while the piece dries
the cut base must be wider than the piece
a plaster cast makes it possible to copy the shape once the surface is dry
text: Wake the clay up before anything else. It comes out of the bag cold and closed, and it gives way only once your palms have worked it over, slowly, without forcing. Air comes next. Slam the mass down on a hard bench, again and again, and listen for the ring to go flat and dull, which is how you know the bubbles are gone. Now open the form. Your thumbs sink in at the center while your fingers travel up the outside and coax the wall taller. Then comes the part that impatience ruins. Dry the piece in the shade, under a damp cloth, well away from any draft that would pull the water out of one side first. Cut the base wider than the body, because anything meant to stand needs an honest footing. Want a copy? Take a plaster cast, but hold off until the surface feels dry against your hand.

units: the window was taken down panel by panel
every element was plotted on a measured drawing before it was removed
the glass was cleaned with demineralized water in the workshop
the cleaning had to spare the dark painted layer
the broken glass was joined with resin under a magnifying instrument
a resin bond cannot be undone afterward
a second window was set in front of the original to shield it from swings of heat
the new metal network is thinner than the previous one
the reinstallation has to be finished before the cold season
text: Work opened with the window coming down, panel by panel, every piece plotted on a measured drawing before it was eased out of its lead frame. The glass then traveled to the workshop, where a wash of demineralized water lifted the crusted deposits without touching the dark painted layer underneath. The hard part followed. Fractured pieces were joined with resin under a magnifier, a bond that nobody will ever be able to take apart again. The team then settled, after some argument, on an outer glazing, a second window set in front of the original to shield it from swings of heat and from condensation. Reassembly came after that, in fresh lead drawn narrower than the old strips, so the drawing could read again as it once did. The site office says the panels will be back in place before the cold season.

units: the performance room sits on the top floor of an old building
its wooden frame is left exposed
the wood soaks up part of the low sounds and softens harsh tones
the side walls lean slightly
the lean of the walls sends the sound back toward the middle rows
listeners far from the stage hear almost as well as those at the front
the low ceiling shortens the reverberation
spoken voices come through more clearly while large ensembles lose their fullness
the programming mostly holds small groups and readings
text: The room sits under the roof of an old building, and the bare timber frame decides how everything sounds inside it. Wood answers to low notes, taking a share of that energy out of the air and rounding off whatever is harsh in a tone. The side walls lean in a little, which throws the reflections back toward the middle of the seating, so a listener at the rear hears roughly what the front row hears. The low ceiling cuts the other way. It shortens the tail of the reverberation, which sharpens spoken words and thins out anything played by a large group. The programming follows from all of that without much argument. Small ensembles, solo recitals and readings fill the calendar, while heavy forces stay away, because the room would only turn them into a blur. Here the building chooses the repertoire.

units: the largest share of museum collections stays out of the exhibition rooms
a shortage of space and of means explains this situation
one answer is to digitize the stored holdings on a large scale
digitizing makes a piece shut in a drawer visible from far away
another answer is to lend works out for a limited term
these loans help institutions that cannot afford to buy pieces
the writer holds that both answers must be carried out together
the two answers meet different needs
text: Almost everything a museum owns sits in storage, and almost none of it ever comes back up the stairs. This is no secret. What hangs on the walls is a sliver of what the building holds, and the reason is dull rather than sinister: too little room, too few hands, too little money. Two answers keep circulating. Digitize the stores on a large scale, so that a print shut in a drawer can be studied by someone who will never walk through the door. Or send the objects out on loan, for a fixed term, to smaller places that could never afford to buy anything comparable. Both are worth doing, and doing at once, because they satisfy different hungers. One feeds study and curiosity at a distance. The other puts a person in a room with the object itself. Refusing to choose has a price. Letting a whole store sleep has a steeper one.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the craftsman compares his trade to a discipline of patience
he used to draw on a screen
a mistake made on a screen was undone with no consequence
the metal he engraves allows no correction
this constraint made him more demanding, as he sees it
on a screen he worked fast and dropped his difficult ideas
on the plate he thinks before every cut
a cut driven too deep ruins weeks of effort
his daughter is learning to draw on a computer and teases him about his method
text: The engraver in the back workshop calls his trade a patience sport. He spent years drawing on a screen, where a wrong line vanished with a keystroke and cost him nothing whatever. The burin put a stop to that. Metal forgives nothing, he says, laughing, and that is exactly what made him better at the work. He likes setting the two side by side. On the screen he turned out plenty and turned it out fast, but he dropped any idea the moment it fought back. On the plate he sits and thinks before every cut, because one stroke driven too deep throws away weeks of work. His daughter, who is learning to draw on a computer, teases him for it and calls him a cave dweller. He tells her he will teach her engraving once she has learned to wait, and that waiting will look less like a punishment then.

units: the writer keeps three successes and one flaw in this exhibition
the low picture rails force the visitor to step close to the works
this closeness changes how the small formats are perceived
the labels are short and free of jargon
the labels describe a technique instead of commenting on a feeling
a quiet sound track carries workshop noises
these noises stand in for background music
the lighting is too even and flattens the relief of the thick materials
the writer advises a visit late in the day when the sun comes through the high windows
text: Three things carry this show, and one thing drags it down. Start with the hanging itself. The rails sit low, low enough that you have to step in close, and that short distance rewrites how the smaller formats read. Then the labels, cut short and scrubbed of jargon, telling you how a thing was made instead of instructing you on what to feel about it. Then the sound, kept faint, a blade scraping across a palette, the creak of an easel being shoved aside. Workshop noise, in other words, and it makes far better company than any piped music. The flaw is the lighting, spread so evenly across the walls that it flattens every ridge of paint on the heaviest pieces. Come back late in the day, when raking sun reaches in through the upper windows, and you will see what the hanging failed to give you.

units: the writer is writing from a performance hall that is still empty
he arrived late at his first class in the fall
he had sworn never to go back on stage
he came back every week through the cold season
his loyalty came first from stubbornness and then from pleasure
the director of the troupe gave him the part of an old caretaker
that part says little and watches the others
the performance the evening before played to a full house
the person he is writing to had urged him to sign up for the class
the writer invites the person he is writing to the closing performance
text: I am writing to you from the empty hall, before the others arrive. Do you remember my first class, back in the fall? I turned up late, coat still buttoned, swearing afterward that nothing would ever drag me onstage again. Through the cold months I kept turning up regardless, week after week, out of sheer stubbornness at first and afterward out of genuine pleasure. When we began staging, the director of the troupe handed me the old caretaker, the one who says almost nothing and watches everybody else. Last night we played to a full house. I felt the silence close over my first line like water going still. This is not boasting. I am writing because you pushed me toward that class, one evening when I insisted nothing amused me anymore. Come to the closing night. I am keeping you a seat down front.

units: the browning of old paper comes from the raw material itself
a pulp made from wood holds a substance that oxidizes in light and air
this oxidation gives off acids that break down the cellulose
the round brown stains come from excess damp together with spores
a fungus feeds on the size held in the sheet
washing lifts these stains only in part
an alkaline bath cancels the acids that are present
this bath leaves a protective reserve in the sheet
a sealed frame mount limits the warping that travel causes
text: People ask us all the time why an old print turns brown. The answer sits in the fiber. Once the pulp carries wood, it carries lignin along with it, and lignin reacts to light and open air, then gives off acids that eat away at the cellulose. What about the brown stains, the ones with a ring around them? Those need damp air and a few spores. A mold settles in, feeds on the size in the sheet, and leaves a mark that washing will only lighten. So what does a conservation workshop do about it? It deacidifies in an alkaline bath, which cancels the acids already at work and leaves a small buffer stock behind in the paper. And if the work has to travel? It goes into a neutral mount inside a sealed frame, since every shift in the surrounding damp makes the fiber move and deepens the cockling.
